Uxorious describes a husband who is excessively devoted, submissive, or indulgent toward his wife — so much so that it becomes a weakness or a flaw.

The single most important word in that definition is excessively. Normal love, care, and devotion toward a wife do not make someone uxorious. What makes a man uxorious is when that devotion crosses a line into something foolish, blind, or embarrassing — when he cannot say no to her, always puts her wishes above everything else (including his own judgment, dignity, or responsibilities), and is essentially controlled by her without even realising it.

Think of it on a scale:

  • Loving husband → good, healthy, normal.
  • Very devoted husband → still fine, admirable even.
  • Uxorious husband → gone too far. He has become so wrapped up in pleasing his wife that he has lost his own spine, judgment, or independence.

The uxorious husband isn't just in love. He is weak in his love. He is blind in it. He will do whatever his wife says, agree with whatever she thinks, and prioritise her every whim even when it's unreasonable.

This word carries a mildly negative and sometimes gently mocking tone. When someone calls a man uxorious, they are not complimenting him. They are suggesting, with a slightly raised eyebrow, that he is under his wife's thumb — perhaps even that she runs the show and he simply obeys.

That said, it isn't a harsh insult. It's more of a sophisticated, literary way of pointing out a man's excessive softness toward his wife. In some contexts, it can even be used humorously — almost with affection — to describe a man who is charmingly, absurdly devoted.
Who Does This Word Apply To?

This is important: uxorious is a gendered, specific word. It applies only to a husband and his relationship with his wife. You would not use it to describe:

  • A wife being overly devoted to her husband (there are other words for that).
  • A boyfriend and girlfriend.
  • A general love between any two people.

It is specifically about a married man being excessively submissive or indulgent toward his wife. That specificity is part of what makes the word so precise and useful.

These sentences will show you exactly how the word feels in real use:

"He was so uxorious that he cancelled his own surgery to attend his wife's book club dinner."

Here, the excess is clear — skipping medical care for a trivial social event of his wife's is beyond devotion; it is foolishness.

"His friends had stopped inviting him out, knowing his uxorious nature meant he would never come without first getting his wife's approval — and she would never give it."

Here, the uxorious quality has made him socially weak and dependent.

"The king was uxorious to a ruinous degree; he reversed sound laws and appointed unqualified ministers simply because his wife asked him to."

Here, the uxoriousness has real consequences — it leads to bad decisions and harm.

"He smiled at being called uxorious. 'If loving my wife too much is a flaw,' he said, 'I'll live with it.'"

Here, the word is used more gently and humorously, and the man brushes it off as a playful accusation.

Because the word is easy to misuse, it helps to know what it does not mean:

  • It does not simply mean "a man who loves his wife." That is just being a good husband.
  • It does not mean a man who respects his wife's opinion. That is healthy partnership.
  • It does not mean a man who is kind or generous to his wife. That is normal decency.

You need that excess — the loss of independent judgment, the foolishness, the submission — for the word to apply correctly.

The noun form of this word is uxoriousness — meaning the quality or state of being uxorious.

"His uxoriousness was well known around town."
When Would You Actually See This Word?

Uxorious is a formal and somewhat old-fashioned word. You are unlikely to hear it in casual everyday conversation. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic or literary fiction (19th and early 20th century novels in particular).
  • Formal essays or critiques, especially about historical figures or characters.
  • Vocabulary enrichment contexts — word-of-the-day lists, crossword puzzles, advanced dictionaries.
  • Humorous or elevated writing, where a writer reaches for a precise, slightly archaic word to paint a vivid picture of a submissive husband.

If you had to remember just one thing:

Uxorious = a husband who is excessively and weakly devoted to his wife, to a degree that goes beyond love into foolishness or submissiveness.

That's it. Loving your wife is beautiful. Being uxorious is loving her so much, and so blindly, that you lose your own judgment in the process.
